dx: Hepatocellular carcinoma in hepatitis B cirrhosis acquired at birth
case: A 46-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 2-month history of right upper quadrant pain and a 6-kg (13-lb) weight loss. He has chronic hepatitis B infection. His mother also has chronic hepatitis B, and he did not receive hepatitis B vaccine as an infant. He does not drink alcohol. Temperature is 37.2 °C (99.0 °F), pulse is 88/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 122/78 mm Hg. Physical examination shows a firm, nodular liver edge 4 cm below the right costal margin. Platelet count is 96,000/mm3 (150,000 to 400,000), serum albumin is 3.1 g/dL (3.5 to 5.5), and serum alpha-fetoprotein is 1,850 ng/mL (under 10). CT shows a nodular liver with a 7-cm arterially enhancing mass in the right lobe. Diagnosis: hepatocellular carcinoma in cirrhosis from hepatitis B acquired at birth.

questions.stem: His 40-year-old brother also acquired hepatitis B at birth. A liver biopsy specimen from the brother shows chronic hepatitis with mild portal fibrosis and no cirrhosis. Which of the following best explains why the brother still has an increased risk of hepatocellular carcinoma?
options: Integration of viral DNA into hepatocyte chromosomes
Regeneration of hepatocytes within fibrous septal nodules
Viral capture of a host proto-oncogene into the viral genome
Accumulation of misfolded protein in the endoplasmic reticulum
approach: Note that the brother has no cirrhosis, so growth inside cirrhotic regenerative nodules cannot be the main driver.
Recall that HBV is a DNA virus whose genome can insert into host chromosomes.
Link integration and the HBx protein to direct oncogenic effects that act even without cirrhosis.
questions.why: Hepatitis B raises cancer risk even in a liver without cirrhosis. Fragments of HBV DNA integrate into hepatocyte chromosomes, where they can disrupt or activate host genes and cause genomic instability. The viral HBx protein also alters cell signaling and interferes with p53 function. Chronic inflammation with repeated hepatocyte turnover adds further risk. Hepatitis C, an RNA virus with no DNA stage, causes cancer mainly after cirrhosis develops.
whyNot: Correct.
Proliferation inside regenerative nodules drives cancer in cirrhosis from any cause. The brother has no cirrhosis, so this cannot explain his risk.
Capture of a cellular proto-oncogene is how acutely transforming animal retroviruses cause tumors. HBV carries no host oncogene.
Misfolded protein trapped in the endoplasmic reticulum describes alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency (PiZZ), which can lead to cirrhosis and then cancer.

questions.stem: Five years ago, he had fever, abdominal pain after meals, new hypertension, and sudden weakness of left ankle dorsiflexion. Mesenteric angiography showed multiple small aneurysms of medium-sized arteries. Tests for antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies were negative. Which of the following mechanisms most likely caused that illness?
options: Antibodies against neutrophil myeloperoxidase
Granulomatous inflammation of the aortic arch branches
HBsAg-antibody immune complexes in arterial walls
Cold-precipitating IgM rheumatoid factor complexes
approach: Recognize polyarteritis nodosa: medium-vessel vasculitis with microaneurysms, mononeuritis multiplex, and bowel ischemia, with negative ANCA.
Recall that chronic hepatitis B is its classic association.
Link HBV to a type III hypersensitivity: circulating HBsAg-antibody complexes deposit in vessel walls and activate complement.
questions.why: Polyarteritis nodosa is a necrotizing vasculitis of medium-sized muscular arteries, often in the kidneys, gut, and peripheral nerves, with sparing of the lungs. Some cases follow chronic hepatitis B. Complexes of HBsAg and antibody deposit in arterial walls, fix complement, and draw in neutrophils. The same type III mechanism causes HBV-related membranous nephropathy. Hepatocyte injury in hepatitis B, by contrast, comes mainly from cytotoxic CD8 T cells.
whyNot: Anti-myeloperoxidase ANCA marks microscopic polyangiitis, a small-vessel vasculitis that often involves the lungs and glomeruli. ANCA testing was negative here.
Granulomatous inflammation of the aortic arch and its branches is Takayasu arteritis, a large-vessel disease mostly of younger women.
Correct.
Cryoglobulins made of IgM rheumatoid factor bound to IgG cause small-vessel vasculitis, usually with hepatitis C.

questions.stem: His 29-year-old sister is pregnant and is positive for HBsAg and HBeAg. If her infant is infected at birth and receives neither hepatitis B vaccine nor hepatitis B immune globulin, which of the following outcomes is most likely?
options: Fulminant hepatic failure within the first year
Chronic infection persisting into adulthood
Clearance of the virus within 6 months
Lifelong immunity after a mild icteric illness
approach: Note the timing: infection at birth.
Recall that the risk of chronic HBV falls with age at infection, about 90% in neonates versus about 5% in healthy adults.
Predict chronic carriage, which sets up later cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma, as in her brother.
questions.why: The age at infection is the strongest predictor of chronic hepatitis B. About 90% of infected neonates become chronic carriers, compared with about 5% of infected healthy adults. Neonates mount weak T-cell responses to the virus, so infection is usually silent rather than icteric. HBeAg-positive mothers transmit most efficiently, which is why their infants receive vaccine and hepatitis B immune globulin within 12 hours of birth.
whyNot: Fulminant hepatitis is rare, occurring in under 1% of acute HBV infections.
Correct.
Clearance within 6 months is the usual course in infected adults, about 95% of whom recover.
Most infected neonates have no symptoms and do not clear the virus. A symptomatic illness followed by immunity is the typical adult pattern.

topics: Outcomes of hepatitis B by age

questions.stem: He is treated with transarterial chemoembolization, which blocks the hepatic artery branch feeding the tumor. The tumor becomes necrotic, but the surrounding liver tissue survives. Which of the following best explains the survival of the surrounding liver?
options: Glycogen stores that sustain hepatocytes without oxygen
Reverse flow from the hepatic veins into the sinusoids
Low oxygen use by hepatocytes compared with tumor cells
Portal venous inflow that supplies most hepatic blood
approach: Recall the dual blood supply: the portal vein brings about 75% of hepatic blood flow and the hepatic artery about 25%.
Note that hepatocellular carcinoma draws its blood almost entirely from the hepatic artery.
Conclude that blocking an arterial branch starves the tumor while portal blood keeps the normal liver alive.
questions.why: The portal vein delivers about 75% of the blood reaching the liver and about half of its oxygen, and the hepatic artery supplies the rest. Normal hepatocytes therefore survive loss of one arterial branch, which is why hepatic infarction is uncommon. Hepatocellular carcinoma grows its own arterial vessels and depends on the hepatic artery, which is why it enhances in the arterial phase on CT and why arterial embolization kills it selectively. The bile ducts also depend on arterial blood and are the structures most at risk from arterial injury.
whyNot: Hepatic glycogen supports blood glucose between meals. It cannot keep cells alive without oxygen for more than a short time.
Blood flows from the sinusoids into central veins and then the hepatic veins. Flow does not reverse to supply the lobule.
Hepatocytes are metabolically very active and use large amounts of oxygen, which is why zone 3 is sensitive to ischemia.
Correct.

topics: Dual blood supply of the liver

dx: Hepatitis D superinfection with decompensated cirrhosis and hepatorenal syndrome
case: A 37-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department because of a 3-week history of worsening jaundice, abdominal swelling, and confusion. She has injected drugs for 15 years and was told 8 years ago that she had chronic hepatitis B, which had caused no symptoms until now. Temperature is 37.0 °C (98.6 °F), pulse is 96/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 96/58 mm Hg. Physical examination shows jaundice, spider angiomas, shifting dullness, and asterixis. Serum total bilirubin is 7.4 mg/dL (0.1 to 1.2), albumin is 2.5 g/dL (3.5 to 5.5), and INR is 2.1 (0.8 to 1.2). Serum creatinine has risen from 0.8 to 2.6 mg/dL (0.6 to 1.1) over 1 week despite albumin infusion. Urine sodium is under 10 mEq/L, and the urine sediment is bland. HDV RNA is detected in serum. Diagnosis: hepatitis D superinfection with decompensated cirrhosis and hepatorenal syndrome.

questions.stem: Hepatitis D virus has a small circular RNA genome that encodes only the delta antigen. Which of the following best explains why this virus can cause infection only in people who also carry hepatitis B virus?
options: It uses HBsAg as its envelope protein
It uses HBV reverse transcriptase to copy its RNA
It integrates its genome into HBV DNA in the nucleus
It requires HBV core protein to build its capsid
approach: Recall that HDV is a defective virus: it can replicate its RNA but cannot make its own coat.
Identify what it borrows: the hepatitis B surface antigen envelope, which it needs to leave the cell and enter new hepatocytes.
Conclude that HDV infects only people with HBsAg, either as coinfection or superinfection.
questions.why: HDV is a defective RNA virus. Its circular genome replicates in the hepatocyte nucleus using host RNA polymerase and encodes only the delta antigen. To assemble and infect new cells, it wraps itself in HBsAg made by HBV. Without HBsAg in the cell, no infectious HDV particles form. For this reason, vaccination against hepatitis B also prevents hepatitis D.
whyNot: Correct.
HDV copies its RNA with host RNA polymerase and has no DNA stage, so it needs no reverse transcriptase.
HDV RNA does not integrate into HBV DNA or host chromosomes.
The HDV nucleocapsid is built from its own delta antigen. It borrows only the HBV surface protein.

questions.stem: Her sexual partner, who also injects drugs, is tested. Results show HBsAg negative, anti-HBs positive, IgM anti-HBc negative, and IgG anti-HBc positive. Which of the following best describes his hepatitis B status?
options: Chronic infection with low-level replication
Past infection that has resolved
Immunity from vaccination alone
Window period of acute infection
approach: Check HBsAg: negative, so there is no current infection.
Check anti-HBc: IgG anti-HBc means the immune system has met the whole virus in the past, which vaccination does not do.
Check anti-HBs: positive means immunity. Together these show a resolved past infection.
questions.why: Anti-HBc forms only after natural infection, because the vaccine contains HBsAg alone. IgG anti-HBc without IgM shows an infection that is not recent. A negative HBsAg with a positive anti-HBs shows that the virus has been cleared and the person is immune. Because he is immune to HBV, he is also protected from HDV.
whyNot: Chronic infection requires HBsAg that persists for more than 6 months. His HBsAg is negative.
Correct.
Vaccination produces anti-HBs only. A positive anti-HBc shows natural infection.
The window period shows IgM anti-HBc with neither HBsAg nor anti-HBs. He has anti-HBs and no IgM anti-HBc.

questions.stem: Her serum glucose is 92 mg/dL (70 to 100), and serum ammonia is 128 µmol/L (15 to 45). Which of the following best explains her confusion and asterixis?
options: Thiamine deficiency impairing pyruvate dehydrogenase
Unconjugated bilirubin deposited in the basal ganglia
Hypoglycemia from depleted hepatic glycogen stores
Reduced hepatic conversion of ammonia to urea
approach: Rule out hypoglycemia: her glucose is normal.
Note the raised ammonia, a nitrogen waste that the liver normally clears.
Link failing hepatocytes and portosystemic shunting to ammonia reaching the brain, where it causes hepatic encephalopathy with asterixis.
questions.why: Hepatocytes clear ammonia from portal blood by turning it into urea through the urea cycle. In cirrhosis, failing hepatocytes make less urea, and portosystemic shunts let ammonia from the gut bypass the liver altogether. In the brain, astrocytes detoxify ammonia by making glutamine, which swells the cells and disturbs neurotransmission. The result is hepatic encephalopathy, with confusion and a flapping tremor called asterixis. Lactulose lowers ammonia by acidifying the colon, which traps it as ammonium.
whyNot: Thiamine deficiency causes Wernicke encephalopathy, with confusion, ophthalmoplegia, and ataxia. It does not raise ammonia.
Unconjugated bilirubin enters the brain in newborns with severe hyperbilirubinemia, causing kernicterus. It does not explain encephalopathy in an adult with cirrhosis.
Hypoglycemia can occur in liver failure, but her glucose is 92 mg/dL.
Correct.

questions.stem: Two months later, she reports shortness of breath that worsens when she sits up and eases when she lies flat. Arterial PO2 on room air is 61 mm Hg (75 to 100), and a chest x-ray is normal. Echocardiography with agitated saline shows bubbles in the left atrium after 4 cardiac cycles. Which of the following best explains her hypoxemia?
options: Fluid in alveoli from low plasma oncotic pressure
An opening in the atrial septum shunting right to left
Dilated pulmonary capillaries limiting oxygen uptake
Constriction of pulmonary arteries raising pressures
approach: Note dyspnea and hypoxemia that worsen upright, with a normal chest x-ray, in a patient with cirrhosis.
Read the bubble study: bubbles in the left atrium after several beats mean an intrapulmonary shunt, while bubbles within about 3 beats point to an intracardiac shunt.
Name hepatopulmonary syndrome: intrapulmonary vascular dilation causing a shunt-like defect in oxygen uptake.
questions.why: In hepatopulmonary syndrome, excess nitric oxide and other vasodilators produced in advanced liver disease widen the pulmonary capillaries, mainly in the lung bases. Blood moves through these wide vessels too fast and too far from alveolar gas for full oxygen uptake, which behaves like a right-to-left shunt. Sitting up sends more blood to the bases, so oxygenation worsens upright. Both this syndrome and her hepatorenal syndrome arise from the abnormal vasodilation of advanced cirrhosis.
whyNot: Low albumin favors edema, but alveolar fluid would show on chest x-ray and would worsen, not improve, when lying flat.
An atrial septal shunt delivers bubbles to the left atrium within about 3 beats. Delayed bubbles point to the lungs.
Correct.
Pulmonary arterial constriction describes portopulmonary hypertension, a different complication of portal hypertension that causes right heart strain rather than position-dependent hypoxemia.

dx: Submandibular sialolithiasis in an older man
case: A 66-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 2-day history of constant pain and swelling below the left side of his jaw. For 3 months, the same area has swollen painfully during meals and settled over the following hour. He takes hydrochlorothiazide for hypertension. Temperature is 38.2 °C (100.8 °F), pulse is 94/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 138/84 mm Hg. Physical examination shows a tender, firm swelling in the left submandibular triangle. Bimanual palpation of the floor of the mouth reveals a hard nodule, and pus is expressed from the left sublingual papilla beside the lingual frenulum. CT shows a 6-mm calcified stone in the left submandibular duct. Diagnosis: submandibular sialolithiasis with secondary bacterial sialadenitis.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains why his swelling and pain appeared during meals before the infection began?
options: Masseter contraction compressing the gland while chewing
Lymph flow into submandibular nodes rising with eating
Reflex saliva secretion against an obstructed duct
Reflux of oral bacteria into the duct with swallowing
approach: Note the pattern: swelling with meals that settles within an hour.
Recall that the taste and smell of food trigger a parasympathetic reflex that sharply increases salivary flow.
Apply it: saliva made behind a stone cannot drain, so the gland distends and hurts until secretion slows.
questions.why: Eating triggers a reflex through the salivatory nuclei and parasympathetic fibers that greatly increases saliva output. For the submandibular gland, these fibers travel in the chorda tympani and synapse in the submandibular ganglion. When a stone blocks the duct, saliva builds up behind it and stretches the gland capsule, causing pain and swelling at mealtimes. Stasis behind the stone then lets oral bacteria ascend the duct, leading to secondary sialadenitis, as in this patient.
whyNot: Chewing does not compress the submandibular gland, which lies below the mandible away from the masseter. The parotid gland and its duct are the structures that lie on the masseter.
Reactive lymph nodes enlarge with infection, not with each meal, and they do not shrink within an hour.
Correct.
Ascending bacteria cause the later infection. They do not explain brief swelling that comes with each meal and resolves.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old woman has a stone lodged in the duct of her right parotid gland. At which of the following sites should the physician look for pus draining from this duct?
options: Buccal mucosa opposite the upper second molar
Buccal mucosa opposite the lower second molar
Sublingual papilla beside the lingual frenulum
Small openings along the sublingual fold
approach: Trace the parotid duct: it runs forward across the masseter about a finger's breadth below the zygomatic arch.
Follow it as it turns medially and pierces the buccinator.
Locate its opening on the cheek mucosa opposite the upper second molar.
questions.why: The parotid (Stensen) duct crosses the masseter, pierces the buccinator, and opens on a small papilla in the buccal mucosa opposite the upper second molar. The submandibular (Wharton) duct opens at the sublingual papilla beside the lingual frenulum, where this man's pus appeared. The sublingual gland drains mostly through many small ducts along the sublingual fold. Knowing these openings lets the examiner milk each gland and see which duct is affected.
whyNot: Correct.
No major salivary duct opens opposite the lower molars. The parotid duct opens in the upper part of the cheek.
The sublingual papilla is the opening of the submandibular duct, where this man's pus appeared.
The sublingual fold carries the many small ducts of the sublingual gland.

questions.stem: He undergoes excision of the left submandibular gland. After surgery, his tongue deviates to the left when he protrudes it, and taste and general sensation over the tongue are normal. Injury to which of the following nerves best explains this deficit?
options: Left glossopharyngeal nerve
Right hypoglossal nerve
Left lingual nerve
Left hypoglossal nerve
approach: Recall that each genioglossus pushes the tongue forward and toward the opposite side.
If one genioglossus is weak, the healthy side pushes the tongue toward the weak side.
Deviation to the left therefore means a left hypoglossal nerve lesion. This nerve runs deep to the submandibular gland.
questions.why: The hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) supplies all intrinsic and extrinsic tongue muscles except the palatoglossus, which is supplied by the vagus nerve. Each genioglossus protrudes the tongue and pushes it toward the opposite side. With a left CN XII lesion, the intact right genioglossus pushes the tongue toward the left. The hypoglossal nerve passes deep to the submandibular gland, below its duct, so it is at risk in this operation along with the lingual nerve.
whyNot: The glossopharyngeal nerve carries taste and general sensation from the posterior third of the tongue. It does not move the tongue.
A right hypoglossal lesion would make the tongue deviate to the right.
The lingual nerve carries general sensation from the anterior two thirds of the tongue, along with taste through chorda tympani fibers. Both are normal here.
Correct.

topics: Nerves at risk in submandibular surgery

questions.stem: An 81-year-old woman develops painful swelling of the right parotid gland 4 days after hip surgery. She has had poor oral intake, and her mouth is dry. Pus expressed from the parotid duct shows gram-positive cocci in clusters, and the organism is catalase positive and coagulase positive. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
options: Streptococcus pyogenes
Staphylococcus aureus
Staphylococcus epidermidis
Viridans group streptococci
approach: Note the setting: an older, dehydrated patient after surgery with one painful parotid gland and pus at the duct.
Read the lab: gram-positive cocci in clusters that are catalase and coagulase positive.
Name Staphylococcus aureus, the leading cause of acute bacterial parotitis.
questions.why: Acute bacterial parotitis develops when saliva flow drops, as with dehydration, surgery, anticholinergic drugs, or poor oral intake. Bacteria then ascend the parotid duct, and Staphylococcus aureus is the most common cause. Pus at the duct opening and a single tender gland separate it from mumps, which is viral, often bilateral, and produces no pus. Coagulase separates S. aureus from coagulase-negative staphylococci.
whyNot: Streptococcus pyogenes forms chains and is catalase negative.
Correct.
Staphylococcus epidermidis is coagulase negative and mainly infects catheters and prosthetic devices.
Viridans streptococci form chains and are catalase negative. They are oral commensals linked to dental caries and endocarditis.

dx: Hereditary chronic pancreatitis from a PRSS1 mutation in a teenager
case: A 16-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of a 4-month history of bulky, greasy, foul-smelling stools and a 5-kg (11-lb) weight loss. She has had 6 episodes of acute pancreatitis since age 8 years. Her father and paternal grandfather have chronic pancreatitis. She does not drink alcohol. BMI is 17 kg/m2. Sweat chloride is 18 mmol/L (under 30), serum triglycerides are 96 mg/dL (under 150), and serum calcium is 9.4 mg/dL (8.5 to 10.5). Fecal elastase is 42 µg/g (above 200). CT shows diffuse pancreatic calcifications and a dilated, irregular main pancreatic duct. Genetic testing shows a heterozygous gain-of-function mutation in PRSS1, the cationic trypsinogen gene. Diagnosis: hereditary chronic pancreatitis.

questions.stem: Which of the following additional findings is most likely in this patient?
options: Macrocytic anemia from impaired jejunal folate absorption
Prolonged prothrombin time correcting with vitamin K
Microcytic anemia from impaired duodenal iron absorption
Hypercalcemia from increased intestinal calcium uptake
approach: Link the low fecal elastase and steatorrhea to loss of pancreatic lipase.
Recall that vitamins A, D, E, and K need fat digestion and micelles to be absorbed.
Predict vitamin K deficiency, which lowers active factors II, VII, IX, and X and prolongs the prothrombin time until vitamin K is given.
questions.why: Chronic pancreatitis destroys acinar tissue, and steatorrhea appears once lipase output falls below about 10% of normal. Undigested fat carries the fat-soluble vitamins out in the stool. Vitamin K deficiency reduces gamma-carboxylation of factors II, VII, IX, and X, so the prothrombin time lengthens. Her liver is normal, so the defect corrects with parenteral vitamin K. Over time, loss of islets also causes diabetes.
whyNot: Folate is absorbed in the jejunum after brush border enzymes process it. Its absorption does not depend on pancreatic enzymes.
Correct.
Iron absorption in the duodenum depends on gastric acid and the mucosa, not on pancreatic enzymes.
Unabsorbed fatty acids bind calcium in the gut lumen, so steatorrhea lowers calcium absorption. Poor vitamin D absorption adds to this.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains how her PRSS1 mutation causes repeated pancreatic injury?
options: Loss of the trypsin inhibitor that blocks trypsin in acinar cells
Defective chloride channel causing thick ductal secretions
Deficient enteropeptidase activation of trypsinogen
Trypsin that resists breakdown inside acinar cells
approach: Note that PRSS1 encodes cationic trypsinogen and that her mutation is a gain of function.
Recall the normal safeguards: SPINK1 inhibits small amounts of early trypsin, and trypsin breaks itself down by autolysis.
Apply it: mutant trypsin activates more easily or resists autolysis, so active trypsin persists in acinar cells and starts autodigestion.
questions.why: Acute pancreatitis starts when trypsinogen is activated to trypsin inside acinar cells, where trypsin then activates the other proenzymes. Normally, SPINK1 blocks small amounts of early trypsin, and trypsin destroys excess trypsin by autolysis. Common PRSS1 mutations, such as R122H, remove the autolysis site or promote autoactivation, so active trypsin survives. Repeated attacks of acute pancreatitis then lead to fibrosis, calcification, and chronic pancreatitis, with a markedly raised lifetime risk of pancreatic cancer. The trait is autosomal dominant, as seen in her father and grandfather.
whyNot: Loss of the trypsin inhibitor results from SPINK1 mutations, a separate gene. Her mutation is a gain of function in trypsinogen itself.
A defective CFTR chloride channel causes cystic fibrosis. Her normal sweat chloride argues against it.
Enteropeptidase deficiency prevents trypsin activation in the duodenum and causes protein malabsorption, not pancreatitis.
Correct.

questions.stem: A pancreatic biopsy specimen shows dense fibrosis with few remaining acini. Scattered clusters of pale-staining cells that lack zymogen granules and have no connection to ducts remain, each surrounded by a rich network of capillaries. Which of the following is the main function of these cell clusters?
options: Hormone release directly into the blood
Secretion of bicarbonate into the ducts
Secretion of proenzymes into the ducts
Secretion of mucus onto the duct lining
approach: Note the features: pale cells, no zymogen granules, no duct, and a rich capillary network.
Identify the islets of Langerhans, the endocrine part of the pancreas.
Recall that islets release insulin, glucagon, and somatostatin into capillaries, not into ducts.
questions.why: Islets of Langerhans are pale-staining clusters of endocrine cells scattered among the darker acini. They lack ducts and lie within a dense network of fenestrated capillaries, into which beta cells release insulin, alpha cells glucagon, and delta cells somatostatin. Acinar cells, by contrast, have basophilic basal cytoplasm and apical eosinophilic zymogen granules and secrete proenzymes into ducts. Islets are often spared early in chronic pancreatitis, but as fibrosis advances they are lost, and diabetes follows.
whyNot: Correct.
Bicarbonate-rich fluid comes from centroacinar and intercalated duct cells, which form the start of the duct system.
Proenzymes come from acinar cells, which contain zymogen granules and drain into ducts.
Mucus comes from cells lining the larger pancreatic ducts, not from clusters of cells with no duct.

questions.stem: Before enzyme replacement is started, which of the following best explains why her digestion of starch is better preserved than her digestion of fat?
options: Bile salts hydrolyze glycosidic bonds when amylase is lacking
Enterocytes absorb whole starch molecules by endocytosis
Salivary and brush border enzymes break down starch
Gastric acid hydrolyzes most starch before it leaves the stomach
approach: Recall where each nutrient is digested: fat almost entirely by pancreatic lipase, starch by both salivary and pancreatic amylase.
Add the brush border: enzymes such as maltase-glucoamylase and sucrase-isomaltase finish starch digestion.
Conclude that starch has backup enzymes outside the pancreas, while fat has little backup.
questions.why: Starch digestion begins with salivary amylase in the mouth and continues in the swallowed food until gastric acid stops it. Pancreatic amylase normally does most of the work in the duodenum, but brush border enzymes such as maltase-glucoamylase can also release glucose from starch fragments. Fat has much less backup, because gastric lipase handles only a small share of triglyceride digestion. For these reasons, steatorrhea is the dominant sign of pancreatic insufficiency, and carbohydrate maldigestion is milder.
whyNot: Bile salts emulsify fat and form micelles. They have no enzyme activity against starch.
Enterocytes absorb only monosaccharides. Starch must be broken down first.
Correct.
Gastric acid inactivates salivary amylase and does not break down starch to any useful degree.

dx: Celiac disease in a toddler with failure to thrive
case: A 22-month-old girl is brought to the physician because of a 6-month history of loose, pale, foul-smelling stools, poor appetite, and irritability. Cereals and bread were added to her diet at 9 months of age. Her weight has fallen from the 50th to below the 5th percentile. Physical examination shows a distended abdomen and wasted buttocks and thighs. Hemoglobin is 9.1 g/dL (10.5 to 13.5), and mean corpuscular volume is 64 fL (70 to 86). Total serum IgA is normal, and serum IgA anti-tissue transglutaminase antibodies are more than 10 times the upper limit of normal. Duodenal biopsy specimens show villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, and increased intraepithelial lymphocytes. Diagnosis: celiac disease.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains her microcytic anemia?
options: Loss of intrinsic factor from gastric parietal cells
Loss of ileal absorptive surface for cobalamin
Chronic blood loss from colonic mucosal ulcers
Loss of villi where iron is mainly absorbed
approach: Classify the anemia: a low MCV means microcytic anemia, most often from iron deficiency.
Recall that iron is absorbed mainly in the duodenum and proximal jejunum.
Link this to celiac disease, which damages the proximal small bowel most.
questions.why: Celiac disease injures the distal duodenum and proximal jejunum most, which is where dietary iron is absorbed. Villous atrophy removes the absorptive surface, including the DMT1 transporters that take up ferrous iron. Iron deficiency anemia can be the first or only sign, and iron deficiency that does not respond to oral iron should prompt testing for celiac disease. Folate, also absorbed in the jejunum, may be low as well, while B12 absorption in the ileum is usually spared.
whyNot: Loss of intrinsic factor causes B12 deficiency with macrocytic anemia, as in autoimmune gastritis.
Ileal disease, such as Crohn disease or ileal resection, impairs B12 absorption and causes macrocytic anemia.
Celiac disease affects the small bowel, not the colon. Bleeding from colonic ulcers fits inflammatory bowel disease.
Correct.

questions.stem: Her 5-year-old brother eats gluten daily and is well. HLA typing shows that he carries neither HLA-DQ2 nor HLA-DQ8. Which of the following best explains why his risk of celiac disease is very low?
options: His class II molecules bind gliadin peptides poorly
His enterocytes lack tissue transglutaminase activity
His B cells cannot switch to making IgA antibodies
His class I molecules cannot present gliadin to CD8 cells
approach: Recall that celiac disease is driven by CD4 T cells that recognize gliadin peptides on class II MHC.
Note that HLA-DQ2 and DQ8 bind deamidated gliadin peptides with high affinity.
Conclude that without these alleles, gliadin is presented poorly, so the disease almost never develops.
questions.why: Almost all patients with celiac disease carry HLA-DQ2 or HLA-DQ8. These class II molecules have binding pockets that hold deamidated gliadin peptides firmly, so antigen-presenting cells can show them to gluten-specific CD4 T cells. Those T cells make interferon-gamma and help B cells make IgA anti-tissue transglutaminase antibodies. Because the alleles are necessary but not sufficient, a negative HLA test nearly excludes celiac disease, while a positive one shows only susceptibility.
whyNot: Correct.
Tissue transglutaminase is a normal enzyme present in everyone. It does not explain his protection.
Inability to make IgA would remove the antibody marker but not the T-cell disease. Selective IgA deficiency is in fact more common in celiac disease.
Intraepithelial CD8 T cells kill enterocytes in celiac disease, but the disease is driven by gliadin presented on class II DQ2 or DQ8 molecules.

topics: HLA-DQ2 and DQ8 in celiac disease

questions.stem: A 4-month-old boy is seen in the same clinic because of diarrhea, poor weight gain, and generalized edema. Serum albumin is 2.1 g/dL (3.5 to 5.5). Duodenal biopsy specimens are normal. Duodenal fluid collected after hormonal stimulation contains normal amounts of trypsinogen and normal amylase activity but almost no trypsin activity. Which of the following is most likely deficient?
options: Cholecystokinin
Pancreatic secretory trypsin inhibitor
Enteropeptidase
Cationic trypsinogen
approach: Note the clues: protein malabsorption with edema, normal mucosa, and plenty of trypsinogen that is never activated.
Recall that trypsinogen is activated in the duodenum by enteropeptidase from the brush border.
Conclude enteropeptidase deficiency, which leaves all pancreatic proteases inactive.
questions.why: Enteropeptidase is a brush border enzyme of the duodenum that cleaves trypsinogen to trypsin. Trypsin then activates chymotrypsinogen, proelastase, procarboxypeptidase, and more trypsinogen. Without enteropeptidase, the pancreas secretes normal proenzymes that never become active, so protein is poorly digested. Infants present with diarrhea, failure to thrive, low albumin, and edema. The normal mucosa separates this from mucosal diseases such as celiac disease.
whyNot: Low cholecystokinin would reduce output of all pancreatic enzymes. Here trypsinogen and amylase are secreted normally.
Loss of pancreatic secretory trypsin inhibitor (SPINK1) allows too much trypsin activity inside the pancreas and predisposes to pancreatitis.
Correct.
A trypsinogen defect would lower trypsinogen itself. Here trypsinogen is present in normal amounts.

questions.stem: After 3 months on a gluten-free diet, she is growing again, but she still has bloating and loose stools after drinking cow's milk. Which of the following best explains her milk intolerance?
options: Antibodies to tissue transglutaminase cross-reacting with lactase
Loss of lactase from injured villus-tip enterocytes
Ongoing gliadin exposure from proteins in cow's milk
Congenital absence of the SGLT1 glucose-galactose carrier
approach: Note the timing: milk intolerance in a child whose villi were recently flattened.
Recall that lactase sits on the brush border of mature enterocytes near the villus tips.
Conclude secondary lactase deficiency, which resolves as the villi regrow.
questions.why: Lactase is a brush border enzyme made mainly by mature enterocytes on the upper villus. Mucosal injury from celiac disease or viral enteritis removes these cells first, and lactase activity is among the last functions to return as the villi recover. Undigested lactose stays in the lumen, draws water by osmosis, and is fermented by colonic bacteria, causing bloating and loose stools. This secondary lactase deficiency usually resolves within weeks to months after the mucosa heals.
whyNot: Anti-tissue transglutaminase antibodies are a marker of celiac disease. They do not cross-react with lactase.
Correct.
Cow's milk proteins such as casein do not contain gliadin, the gluten protein that drives celiac disease.
Glucose-galactose malabsorption from SGLT1 defects causes severe diarrhea from the first feeds in infancy, not after a period of normal milk intake.

dx: NSAID-induced posterior gastric ulcer perforating into the lesser sac
case: A 72-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department 5 hours after the sudden onset of severe epigastric pain that spreads to her back. She has osteoarthritis and has taken naproxen 500 mg twice daily for 1 year. For 6 weeks, she has had burning epigastric pain that worsens with meals. Temperature is 38.0 °C (100.4 °F), pulse is 112/min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 102/64 mm Hg. Physical examination shows epigastric tenderness with guarding, and the lower abdomen is soft. An upright chest x-ray shows no free air under the diaphragm. CT shows a perforation in the posterior wall of the gastric body, with air and fluid confined to the lesser sac. Helicobacter pylori stool antigen testing is negative. Diagnosis: NSAID-induced gastric ulcer perforated into the lesser sac.

questions.stem: Which of the following changes in gastric mucosal defense most directly caused her ulcer?
options: Hypergastrinemia expanding the parietal cell mass
Ammonia from bacterial urease injuring surface cells
Less mucus, bicarbonate, and mucosal blood flow
Delayed gastric emptying prolonging acid exposure
approach: Identify the cause: daily NSAID use with a negative H. pylori test.
Recall that NSAIDs inhibit COX-1, which makes protective prostaglandins in the gastric mucosa.
Link loss of prostaglandins to weaker mucosal defenses, so normal amounts of acid can injure the mucosa.
questions.why: Prostaglandins E2 and I2, made by COX-1 in the stomach, stimulate mucus and bicarbonate secretion, maintain mucosal blood flow, and modestly reduce acid secretion. NSAIDs block COX and remove this protection, so even normal amounts of acid and pepsin can cause ulcers. Gastric ulcers typically hurt more with meals, while duodenal ulcer pain often eases with food. Gastric ulcers also need biopsy, because a minority are malignant.
whyNot: Hypergastrinemia from a gastrinoma (Zollinger-Ellison syndrome) expands parietal cell mass and causes multiple ulcers, often in the duodenum or jejunum.
Urease-generated ammonia is one way H. pylori damages the mucosa. Her H. pylori test is negative.
Correct.
Slow gastric emptying is not how NSAIDs injure the mucosa. NSAID ulcers arise from loss of prostaglandin protection.

questions.stem: On the same day, a 58-year-old man with cirrhotic ascites is admitted with fever and diffuse abdominal tenderness without rigidity. Paracentesis shows 480 neutrophils/mm3 (under 250). Compared with this woman's peritonitis, which of the following findings is most likely in his peritoneal fluid?
options: Mixed aerobic and anaerobic bacteria from bowel
Acid-fast bacilli with mainly lymphocytes
Fungal and bacterial growth from gastric contents
A single species of enteric gram-negative rod
approach: Recognize spontaneous bacterial peritonitis: cirrhotic ascites, fever, and 250 or more neutrophils/mm3 with no perforation.
Recall that SBP comes from bacteria translocating from the gut, so usually one organism grows.
Contrast this with secondary peritonitis from a perforated viscus, which is polymicrobial.
questions.why: Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis infects ascites without a hole in the bowel. Gut bacteria cross the wall into lymph and blood and seed the ascitic fluid, and culture usually grows a single organism, most often Escherichia coli or Klebsiella. Secondary peritonitis follows perforation of a viscus, spills many organisms at once, and causes a rigid abdomen. A polymicrobial culture in a patient with ascites suggests a perforation rather than SBP.
whyNot: Mixed aerobes and anaerobes point to secondary peritonitis from a perforated bowel, as with diverticulitis or appendicitis.
Acid-fast bacilli with lymphocyte-rich fluid suggest tuberculous peritonitis, which develops over weeks.
Mixed bacterial and Candida growth fits peritonitis after a gastric or upper gut perforation, like this woman's, not SBP.
Correct.

questions.stem: Repeat CT 1 day later shows that air and fluid have passed from the lesser sac into the right subhepatic space through the natural opening between the two peritoneal sacs. Which of the following structures forms the anterior boundary of this opening?
options: Hepatoduodenal ligament
Hepatogastric ligament
Caudate lobe of the liver
Gastrosplenic ligament
approach: Name the opening: the omental (epiploic) foramen connects the lesser sac to the greater sac.
Recall its boundaries: the hepatoduodenal ligament in front, the inferior vena cava behind, the caudate lobe above, and the first part of the duodenum below.
Pick the anterior boundary, which contains the portal triad.
questions.why: The omental foramen (of Winslow) is the only natural connection between the lesser and greater sacs. Its anterior wall is the free edge of the lesser omentum, the hepatoduodenal ligament, which holds the portal vein, proper hepatic artery, and common bile duct. Its posterior wall is the inferior vena cava, its roof is the caudate lobe, and its floor is the first part of the duodenum. Surgeons compress the hepatoduodenal ligament through this foramen (the Pringle maneuver) to control bleeding from the liver.
whyNot: Correct.
The hepatogastric ligament is the part of the lesser omentum between the liver and the lesser curvature. It forms part of the anterior wall of the lesser sac, not of the foramen.
The caudate lobe forms the roof of the omental foramen.
The gastrosplenic ligament forms part of the left boundary of the lesser sac.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man in the intensive care unit after a severe traumatic brain injury with raised intracranial pressure develops upper gastrointestinal bleeding. Endoscopy shows an ulcer in the proximal duodenum. Which of the following mechanisms most likely caused this ulcer?
options: Mucosal ischemia from hypovolemic shock
Vagally driven increase in acid secretion
Bile reflux through an incompetent pylorus
Loss of mucosal prostaglandins from COX inhibition
approach: Note the setting: severe brain injury with raised intracranial pressure.
Recall the Cushing ulcer, a stress ulcer linked to brain injury.
Link raised intracranial pressure to stimulation of the vagal nuclei, which increases gastric acid output.
questions.why: Cushing ulcers develop after severe brain injury or raised intracranial pressure. Stimulation of the vagal nuclei increases acetylcholine release onto parietal cells, and acid output rises. They differ from Curling ulcers after severe burns, where hypovolemia and mucosal ischemia are the main problem. Both are forms of stress-related mucosal injury seen in critically ill patients.
whyNot: Mucosal ischemia from hypovolemia is the main mechanism of Curling ulcers after severe burns and of stress ulcers in shock.
Correct.
Bile reflux causes chemical gastritis, most often after gastric surgery.
Loss of prostaglandins explains NSAID injury, as in this woman.

dx: Intestinal-type gastric adenocarcinoma from chronic Helicobacter pylori pangastritis
case: A 66-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 4-month history of early satiety, epigastric discomfort, and a 9-kg (20-lb) weight loss. His diet has long been rich in smoked and salt-preserved meats and fish. He was told 20 years ago that he had a stomach infection but did not complete treatment. Hemoglobin is 10.2 g/dL (13.5 to 17.5), and mean corpuscular volume is 75 fL (80 to 100). Upper endoscopy shows an ulcerated mass on the lesser curvature of the antrum, with thin, pale mucosa throughout the antrum and body. Biopsy specimens of the mass show gland-forming adenocarcinoma. The surrounding mucosa shows atrophy, intestinal metaplasia, and curved rods in the surface mucus. Diagnosis: intestinal-type gastric adenocarcinoma from chronic Helicobacter pylori pangastritis.

questions.stem: Physical examination shows a firm, nontender, 2-cm lymph node in the left supraclavicular fossa. Which of the following routes best explains spread of the tumor to this site?
options: Portal venous drainage to the liver and beyond
Lymphatic drainage through the thoracic duct
Seeding of tumor cells across the peritoneum
Direct extension through the diaphragm
approach: Identify the node: a left supraclavicular (Virchow) node.
Recall that lymph from the abdomen rises in the thoracic duct, which empties at the junction of the left subclavian and internal jugular veins.
Conclude lymphatic spread along the thoracic duct.
questions.why: Lymph from the stomach drains to the celiac nodes and then to the cisterna chyli and thoracic duct. The thoracic duct ends at the left venous angle, beside the left supraclavicular nodes, so abdominal cancers can spread there and form a Virchow node. Other classic signs of spread from gastric cancer are a periumbilical nodule (Sister Mary Joseph nodule) and ovarian metastases (Krukenberg tumor), which are most typical of the diffuse signet ring cell type.
whyNot: Portal venous spread carries tumor to the liver, producing hepatic metastases rather than a neck node.
Correct.
Peritoneal seeding produces carcinomatosis, ascites, ovarian deposits, or a mass in the rectouterine or rectovesical pouch.
Direct extension spreads to adjacent organs such as the pancreas, colon, or liver, not to the neck.

questions.stem: Two months before endoscopy, a urea breath test was negative while he was taking omeprazole 40 mg daily for dyspepsia. Which of the following best explains the false-negative result?
options: Fewer organisms and less urease during acid suppression
Breath testing detects serum antibodies, which wane over time
Intestinal metaplasia breaking down the labeled urea first
Antral organisms lacking urease, unlike organisms in the body
approach: Recall how the test works: the patient swallows labeled urea, and H. pylori urease splits it into ammonia and labeled CO2, which is exhaled.
Note that proton pump inhibitors suppress the organism and reduce its numbers and urease activity.
Conclude a false-negative test, which is why proton pump inhibitors are stopped about 2 weeks before breath or stool antigen testing.
questions.why: Helicobacter pylori is a curved, flagellated, microaerophilic gram-negative rod. Its urease splits urea into ammonia and CO2, buffering acid around the organism, and the urea breath test detects the labeled CO2. Proton pump inhibitors, bismuth, and recent antibiotics reduce the number of organisms and their urease activity, so breath tests and stool antigen tests can be falsely negative. Biopsy with histology, as in this patient, can still show the organisms.
whyNot: Correct.
The breath test detects active urease, not antibodies. Serology detects antibodies and cannot separate current from past infection.
Metaplastic intestinal cells do not split urea. Only bacterial urease releases labeled CO2 in this test.
All H. pylori strains make large amounts of urease, wherever they live in the stomach.

questions.stem: His sister has megaloblastic anemia, antibodies to intrinsic factor, and chronic atrophic gastritis confined to the gastric body and fundus. Which of the following findings is most likely shared by his gastritis and hers?
options: Curved gram-negative rods in the surface mucus
Antral sparing with preserved gastrin-producing cells
Risk of MALT lymphoma from chronic B-cell stimulation
Intestinal metaplasia of the atrophic mucosa
approach: Identify her disease: autoimmune gastritis of the body and fundus with pernicious anemia.
Compare the two: H. pylori gastritis starts in the antrum and may spread to the body, while autoimmune gastritis spares the antrum.
Find the shared feature: both cause chronic atrophy with intestinal metaplasia and a raised risk of adenocarcinoma.
questions.why: Chronic H. pylori gastritis usually begins in the antrum and in some patients spreads to the body as pangastritis. Autoimmune gastritis targets parietal cells in the body and fundus and spares the antrum. Long-standing injury in either disease leads to mucosal atrophy and intestinal metaplasia, with goblet cells replacing gastric glands, which raises the risk of gastric adenocarcinoma. H. pylori also raises the risk of MALT lymphoma, while autoimmune gastritis raises the risk of carcinoid tumors from ECL cell hyperplasia.
whyNot: Curved gram-negative rods are seen only in H. pylori gastritis.
Antral sparing is a feature of autoimmune gastritis. His antrum is involved.
MALT lymphoma arises from lymphoid tissue driven by H. pylori and is not a feature of autoimmune gastritis.
Correct.

questions.stem: Gastric fluid aspirated at endoscopy has a pH of 7.0 (normal fasting pH under 3). He also reports bloating and loose stools, and a glucose hydrogen breath test shows an early rise in breath hydrogen. Which of the following best explains these symptoms?
options: Rapid gastric emptying into the small bowel
Reduced pancreatic bicarbonate output
Loss of the acid barrier to swallowed bacteria
Loss of migrating motor complexes after vagal injury
approach: Note the gastric pH of 7.0: atrophic pangastritis has destroyed the parietal cells, causing achlorhydria.
Recall that gastric acid kills most swallowed bacteria.
Link achlorhydria to small intestinal bacterial overgrowth, in which bacteria ferment glucose high in the small bowel and raise breath hydrogen early.
questions.why: Gastric acid is a major barrier against swallowed microbes. When chronic H. pylori pangastritis or autoimmune gastritis destroys parietal cells, the stomach stops making acid. More bacteria survive into the small intestine, where they ferment carbohydrates, deconjugate bile salts, and take up vitamin B12, causing bloating and diarrhea. Achlorhydria also impairs iron absorption, because acid helps keep dietary iron soluble and in the ferrous form, and it removes the negative feedback of acid on gastrin release.
whyNot: Rapid emptying (dumping) follows gastric surgery and causes symptoms soon after meals, but it does not cause bacterial overgrowth.
Pancreatic bicarbonate output does not control the number of bacteria in the small bowel.
Correct.
Loss of migrating motor complexes can cause bacterial overgrowth, but he has no vagal injury, and his stomach makes no acid.

dx: Rotavirus gastroenteritis with dehydration in an unvaccinated infant
case: A 9-month-old boy is brought to the emergency department in January because of 3 days of vomiting followed by frequent watery, nonbloody diarrhea, about 10 stools daily. He attends daycare, where several infants have had similar illnesses. His parents declined routine childhood vaccines. Temperature is 38.3 °C (100.9 °F), pulse is 168/min, respirations are 40/min, and blood pressure is 78/46 mm Hg. He is lethargic. Physical examination shows sunken eyes, dry mucous membranes, and a capillary refill time of 3 seconds. Serum sodium is 134 mEq/L (135 to 145), and serum bicarbonate is 15 mEq/L (22 to 28). Stool antigen testing is positive for rotavirus. Diagnosis: rotavirus gastroenteritis with moderate to severe dehydration.

questions.stem: One licensed vaccine against this virus contains reassortant viruses that combine human genes for outer capsid proteins with the remaining genes of a bovine strain. Which of the following features of the virus makes such reassortants possible?
options: A lipid envelope from the host cell membrane
A reverse transcriptase that copies RNA into DNA
A single positive-sense RNA that serves as mRNA
A genome divided into separate RNA segments
approach: Recall the rotavirus genome: 11 segments of double-stranded RNA inside a nonenveloped, triple-layered capsid.
Note that when two strains infect one cell, whole segments can be swapped.
Link segment swapping (reassortment) to the design of a human-bovine reassortant vaccine.
questions.why: Rotavirus is a nonenveloped reovirus with 11 segments of double-stranded RNA. When two strains infect the same cell, their segments can mix and produce reassortant progeny. Vaccine makers used this to place human genes for the outer capsid proteins VP7 and VP4 on a bovine strain that is naturally attenuated in humans. The vaccine therefore raises protective antibodies without causing disease. Segmented genomes also allow reassortment in influenza virus, which drives antigenic shift.
whyNot: Rotavirus has no envelope, which helps it survive on hands and surfaces. An envelope does not allow gene swapping.
Reverse transcriptase is used by retroviruses and hepatitis B virus. Rotavirus copies its genome with its own RNA-dependent RNA polymerase.
A single positive-sense RNA genome describes enteroviruses and caliciviruses such as norovirus, which do not reassort.
Correct.

questions.stem: His 34-year-old father recently returned from a 2-week business trip to a country with limited water treatment. On the fourth day of the trip, after eating salads and drinking tap water, he had 4 to 6 watery, nonbloody stools daily with cramps and no fever. The illness resolved in 3 days without treatment. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the father's illness?
options: Bacillus cereus
Enterotoxigenic E. coli
Vibrio cholerae O1
Clostridium perfringens
approach: Note the setting: a traveler to an area with poor sanitation, with watery diarrhea a few days after arrival.
Note the mild course: a few stools a day, no blood, no fever, and recovery on its own.
Match this to enterotoxigenic E. coli, the most common cause of traveler's diarrhea.
questions.why: Enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli is the leading cause of traveler's diarrhea. It spreads through food and water contaminated with feces, attaches to the small bowel with fimbriae, and makes heat-labile and heat-stable toxins that cause watery secretory diarrhea without invasion. The illness usually lasts a few days and resolves on its own. Cholera causes far larger volumes of rice-water stool and is uncommon in travelers.
whyNot: Bacillus cereus causes vomiting within a few hours, or diarrhea within about 8 to 16 hours, after reheated rice or other stored foods.
Correct.
Vibrio cholerae causes profuse rice-water diarrhea that can lead to shock within hours, mostly where cholera outbreaks occur.
Clostridium perfringens causes watery diarrhea and cramps about 8 to 16 hours after eating meat dishes kept warm for hours, and it lasts about a day.

questions.stem: Before coming to the hospital, his parents gave him apple juice, which is high in fructose and low in sodium, and his diarrhea worsened. Which of the following best explains why this juice is a poor substitute for oral rehydration solution?
options: Fructose blocks SGLT1 on the brush border
Fructose needs lactase for its absorption
Fructose enters by GLUT5 without sodium
Fructose is absorbed only in the colon
approach: Recall how oral rehydration solution works: SGLT1 carries sodium with glucose, and water follows the absorbed solute.
Recall how fructose is absorbed: facilitated diffusion through GLUT5 with no sodium, then GLUT2 into the blood.
Conclude that fructose-rich, low-sodium juice does not drive sodium and water uptake, and the unabsorbed sugar adds an osmotic load.
questions.why: Glucose and galactose cross the brush border on SGLT1 together with sodium, so a glucose-sodium solution pulls sodium and water into the body even during infectious diarrhea. Fructose enters by GLUT5, a facilitated transporter that carries no sodium and has limited capacity. All three sugars leave across the basolateral membrane through GLUT2. Juice high in fructose and low in sodium therefore adds little sodium uptake, and the fructose that is not absorbed stays in the lumen and holds water there, making the diarrhea worse.
whyNot: Fructose does not block SGLT1. It uses a separate transporter.
Lactase splits lactose into glucose and galactose. Fructose is a monosaccharide and needs no brush border enzyme.
Correct.
Fructose is absorbed in the small intestine. Only the part that escapes absorption reaches the colon.

questions.stem: At a family picnic, his 6-year-old cousin eats ham and potato salad that sat in the sun for several hours. Three hours later, she develops nausea and repeated vomiting without fever, and she recovers within a day. Which of the following best explains the rapid onset of her illness?
options: Ingestion of a heat-stable toxin already formed in food
Toxin made by bacteria after they colonize the small bowel
Bacterial invasion of the colonic mucosa
Toxin that glucosylates Rho proteins in colonocytes
approach: Note the timing: vomiting within a few hours of eating.
Recall that onset this fast means the toxin was already in the food, because there was no time for bacteria to grow in the gut.
Match ham and potato salad left warm to Staphylococcus aureus enterotoxin.
questions.why: Staphylococcus aureus from a food handler's skin grows in protein-rich foods such as ham, egg, or potato salad kept warm. It releases enterotoxins that resist heat and stomach acid. These preformed toxins stimulate vagal pathways to the vomiting center within about 1 to 6 hours, cause prominent vomiting, and clear within about a day. The emetic toxin of Bacillus cereus works the same way after reheated rice.
whyNot: Correct.
Toxins made after colonization, such as cholera toxin and the heat-labile toxin of ETEC, raise cAMP and cause watery diarrhea after an incubation of a day or more.
Invasion of the colonic mucosa by Shigella or Campylobacter causes fever and bloody diarrhea after 1 to 3 days or longer.
Toxins A and B of Clostridioides difficile glucosylate Rho GTPases and cause colitis, usually after antibiotic use.

dx: Yersinia enterocolitica mesenteric adenitis mimicking appendicitis in a man with hereditary hemochromatosis
case: A 34-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of a 3-day history of fever, watery diarrhea, and pain in the right lower abdomen. Four days before the illness began, he ate undercooked pork. Two months ago, he was diagnosed with hereditary hemochromatosis (homozygous HFE C282Y) and has not yet begun phlebotomy. Temperature is 38.6 °C (101.5 °F), pulse is 104/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 124/76 mm Hg. Physical examination shows right lower quadrant tenderness. Leukocyte count is 14,200/mm3 (4,500 to 11,000), serum ferritin is 2,100 ng/mL (24 to 336), and transferrin saturation is 78% (20 to 50). CT shows a normal appendix, a thickened terminal ileum, and enlarged mesenteric lymph nodes. Stool culture grows Yersinia enterocolitica. Diagnosis: Yersinia mesenteric adenitis mimicking appendicitis in a man with iron overload.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains why his pain and tenderness are localized to the right lower quadrant?
options: Invasion of ileal Peyer patches and draining nodes
Obstruction of the appendiceal lumen by lymphoid tissue
Inflammation of a Meckel diverticulum in the ileum
Toxin-mediated necrosis of the cecal wall
approach: Note the clues: a thickened terminal ileum and enlarged mesenteric nodes with a normal appendix.
Recall that Yersinia crosses the epithelium through M cells over Peyer patches, which are most numerous in the terminal ileum.
Link this to spread into the mesenteric lymph nodes of the right lower quadrant, which mimics appendicitis.
questions.why: Yersinia enterocolitica binds M cells over Peyer patches with its invasin protein and crosses into the lymphoid tissue. Peyer patches are most numerous in the terminal ileum, and the organisms then reach the mesenteric lymph nodes that drain it. Inflamed ileum and nodes in the right lower quadrant produce fever and localized pain, a picture called pseudoappendicitis. Iron overload and deferoxamine therapy raise the risk of severe Yersinia infection because the organism thrives when extra iron is available.
whyNot: Correct.
Lymphoid hyperplasia can block the appendix and cause appendicitis, but CT shows a normal appendix.
Meckel diverticulitis can mimic appendicitis, but it does not explain ileal thickening with enlarged nodes and a stool culture growing Yersinia.
Necrosis of the cecal wall is not a feature of Yersinia infection. Neutropenic enterocolitis (typhlitis) affects the cecum in patients with very low neutrophil counts.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old woman has pain that began around the umbilicus and, 14 hours later, became sharp and localized to the right lower quadrant, where she has guarding and rebound tenderness. Surgery confirms acute appendicitis. Which of the following best explains the change in the character and location of her pain?
options: Rising luminal pressure stretching the appendix wall
Spread of infection into mesenteric lymph nodes
Inflammation reaching the parietal peritoneum
Irritation of the obturator internus muscle
approach: Recall that early pain from the appendix is visceral: dull, poorly localized, and felt around the umbilicus.
Note the change to sharp, well-localized pain with rebound tenderness.
Link this to inflammation spreading through the wall to the parietal peritoneum, which has somatic innervation and localizes pain precisely.
questions.why: Obstruction of the appendix lumen raises pressure, stretches the wall, and leads to ischemia and bacterial invasion. At first, only visceral afferents are stimulated, so the pain is vague and periumbilical. When inflammation reaches the serosa and touches the parietal peritoneum, somatic nerves of the abdominal wall are stimulated. These give sharp pain near McBurney point, with guarding and rebound tenderness. Pain that later spreads across the abdomen suggests perforation.
whyNot: Wall distension stimulates visceral afferents, which produce the early dull periumbilical pain, not sharp localized pain.
Mesenteric node involvement is typical of Yersinia infection, as in this man. It does not explain the shift from vague to sharp, localized pain in appendicitis.
Correct.
Irritation of the obturator internus by a pelvic appendix causes pain on internal rotation of the flexed hip (obturator sign). It does not explain the shift in her pain.

questions.stem: His 30-year-old sister is well. Genetic testing shows that both of their parents are heterozygous for HFE C282Y. Which of the following is the probability that his sister is homozygous for this mutation?
approach: Recall that hereditary hemochromatosis from HFE C282Y is autosomal recessive.
With two heterozygous parents, each child has a 1 in 4 chance of inheriting two mutant alleles.
Note that being well at 30 does not exclude homozygosity, because women often show iron overload later than men.
questions.why: HFE hemochromatosis is autosomal recessive. With two carrier parents, each child has a 25% chance of being homozygous, a 50% chance of being a carrier, and a 25% chance of having two normal alleles. Homozygotes have inappropriately low hepcidin, so enterocytes and macrophages release too much iron through ferroportin. Women often present a decade or more later than men because menstruation and pregnancy remove iron. Penetrance is incomplete, so siblings are screened with iron studies and genotyping.
whyNot: A risk of zero would apply only if at least one parent carried no mutant allele.
Correct.
Fifty percent is the chance that she is a heterozygous carrier, or the risk to each child of a parent with an autosomal dominant disorder.
Two thirds is the chance that an unaffected sibling is a carrier, once homozygosity has been excluded.

questions.stem: A coworker develops cramping abdominal pain and bloody diarrhea 3 days after eating undercooked chicken. Two weeks after the diarrhea resolves, he develops symmetric weakness that ascends from the feet, with absent deep tendon reflexes. Which of the following organisms most likely caused his diarrheal illness?
options: Shigella sonnei
Escherichia coli O157:H7
Entamoeba histolytica
Campylobacter jejuni
approach: Recognize Guillain-Barre syndrome: ascending symmetric weakness with areflexia after an infection.
Recall that Campylobacter jejuni is the infection most often linked to it.
Confirm with the exposure: undercooked poultry and bloody diarrhea fit Campylobacter.
questions.why: Campylobacter jejuni is a common bacterial cause of bloody diarrhea after undercooked poultry and the infection most often linked to Guillain-Barre syndrome. Lipooligosaccharide on some strains resembles gangliosides on peripheral nerves. Antibodies made against the bacterium then cross-react with the nerves, a process called molecular mimicry. Campylobacter can also trigger reactive arthritis, like other invasive enteric bacteria.
whyNot: Shigella causes bloody diarrhea that spreads person to person. Its later complications include reactive arthritis and, with Shigella dysenteriae type 1, hemolytic uremic syndrome.
E. coli O157:H7, usually from undercooked ground beef, causes bloody diarrhea followed by hemolytic uremic syndrome, mostly in children.
Entamoeba histolytica causes amebic dysentery and liver abscess, not Guillain-Barre syndrome.
Correct.

dx: Giardiasis with steatorrhea in a backpacker after drinking stream water
case: A 27-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 10-day history of bloating, abdominal cramps, flatulence, sulfur-smelling belches, and greasy, foul-smelling stools that float. She has lost 3 kg (6.6 lb). Her symptoms began 1 week after she drank untreated water from mountain streams on a backpacking trip. She has had no blood in her stools. Temperature is 37.0 °C (98.6 °F), pulse is 78/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 112/70 mm Hg. Physical examination shows a mildly distended, nontender abdomen. Stool antigen testing is positive for Giardia lamblia. Diagnosis: giardiasis with steatorrhea.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains why her illness causes fatty, nonbloody stools without fever?
options: Larvae that penetrate the bowel wall and migrate to the lungs
Trophozoites that invade the colon and form flask-shaped ulcers
Trophozoites that attach to villi without invading the mucosa
Acid-fast oocysts developing within enterocyte membranes
approach: Recall the life cycle: she swallowed cysts in stream water, and they released trophozoites in the duodenum.
Recall that Giardia trophozoites cling to the brush border with a ventral adhesive disk but do not invade.
Link attachment without invasion to malabsorption with fatty stools and no blood or fever.
questions.why: Giardia cysts survive in cold water and resist usual chlorine levels. In the duodenum, each cyst releases trophozoites that attach to the villi with a ventral adhesive disk. They damage the brush border and impair absorption, but they do not invade, so there is no blood, no pus, and usually no fever. The result is bloating, foul greasy stools, and sometimes secondary lactase deficiency. IgA deficiency increases the risk of chronic infection.
whyNot: Larvae that penetrate the bowel and travel to the lungs describe Strongyloides, which can cause autoinfection and hyperinfection.
Flask-shaped colonic ulcers come from Entamoeba histolytica, which causes bloody diarrhea and liver abscess.
Correct.
Acid-fast oocysts describe Cryptosporidium, Cyclospora, and Cystoisospora, which cause watery diarrhea that is severe in people with AIDS.

questions.stem: While she recovers, a dietitian suggests replacing some dietary fat with medium-chain triglyceride oil. Which of the following best explains why medium-chain fatty acids are absorbed well even when long-chain fat absorption is impaired?
options: They are packaged with apoB-48 more quickly
They enter enterocytes with sodium through SGLT1
They need no lipase before entering the lacteals
They pass to portal blood without chylomicrons
approach: Trace long-chain fat absorption: micelles deliver fatty acids and monoglycerides to the enterocyte, where they are re-esterified, packaged with apoB-48 into chylomicrons, and sent into lacteals.
Contrast medium-chain fatty acids: they are more water soluble, depend less on micelles, and are not packaged into chylomicrons.
Conclude that they pass directly into portal blood bound to albumin, bypassing the steps that fail in malabsorption.
questions.why: Long-chain fatty acids and 2-monoglycerides need bile salt micelles to reach the brush border. Inside the enterocyte, they are rebuilt into triglycerides in the smooth endoplasmic reticulum, packaged with apoB-48 into chylomicrons, and exported into lacteals and then the thoracic duct. Medium-chain fatty acids are more water soluble, need fewer of these steps, and pass from the enterocyte straight into portal blood. That is why medium-chain triglycerides help patients with fat malabsorption or with defects in chylomicron formation.
whyNot: Medium-chain fatty acids are mostly not packaged into chylomicrons at all. Long-chain fatty acids are the ones packaged with apoB-48.
SGLT1 carries glucose and galactose with sodium. Fatty acids cross the membrane by diffusion and fatty acid transporters.
Medium-chain fatty acids go to the portal vein, not the lacteals. Lacteals receive chylomicrons.
Correct.

questions.stem: Her travel companion did not drink stream water but ate undercooked eggs at a roadside restaurant. He develops fever, cramps, and diarrhea with some blood. Stool culture grows a motile gram-negative rod that does not ferment lactose and produces hydrogen sulfide. Which of the following organisms is most likely responsible?
options: Salmonella enterica
Shigella sonnei
Campylobacter jejuni
Escherichia coli O157:H7
approach: Use the exposure: undercooked eggs point to nontyphoidal Salmonella.
Use the lab features: a motile, non-lactose-fermenting gram-negative rod that makes hydrogen sulfide.
Separate it from Shigella, which is nonmotile and makes no hydrogen sulfide.
questions.why: Nontyphoidal Salmonella enterica, such as serotype Enteritidis, is spread by poultry, eggs, and reptiles. It is a motile gram-negative rod that does not ferment lactose and produces hydrogen sulfide, which shows as black colonies on selective media. It needs a fairly large dose to cause disease, because stomach acid kills many organisms. It invades the ileal and colonic mucosa and causes fever and diarrhea that is sometimes bloody.
whyNot: Correct.
Shigella is nonmotile, makes no hydrogen sulfide, and needs only 10 to 100 organisms, so it spreads from person to person.
Campylobacter jejuni is a comma-shaped rod that grows best at 42 °C (107.6 °F) and comes mainly from undercooked poultry.
E. coli O157:H7 ferments lactose, does not ferment sorbitol, and comes mainly from undercooked ground beef.

questions.stem: Her 33-year-old brother has had bloating and loose stools after dairy foods since his late teens. Small bowel biopsy specimens are normal, and a lactose hydrogen breath test is positive. Which of the following best explains his condition?
options: Loss of villus-tip enterocytes after mucosal injury
Programmed decline in lactase gene expression
Absent SGLT1 glucose-galactose cotransporter
Autoantibodies against brush border enzymes
approach: Note the normal biopsy, which excludes damage to the villi.
Note onset after childhood, with symptoms only after dairy.
Conclude primary (adult-type) lactase deficiency, in which lactase expression falls after weaning by a genetically programmed process.
questions.why: In most of the world's population, intestinal lactase activity falls after early childhood because expression of the lactase gene is turned down. This is primary, or adult-type, lactase deficiency, and the villi are normal. Undigested lactose holds water in the lumen and is fermented by colonic bacteria to gases and short-chain fatty acids, causing bloating and loose stools. Secondary lactase deficiency, by contrast, follows mucosal injury, as after giardiasis or celiac disease, and improves when the villi recover.
whyNot: Loss of villus-tip enterocytes causes secondary lactase deficiency after mucosal injury. His biopsy is normal.
Correct.
SGLT1 defects cause glucose-galactose malabsorption with severe diarrhea from the first weeks of life.
Autoantibodies against brush border enzymes are not a recognized cause of lactase deficiency.
